summary: This document proposes additional RADIUS attributes for dynamic VLAN assignment and prioritization, used when provisioning access to IEEE 802 local networks. The attributes can be used in either RADIUS or Diameter.

eli5.summary: When someone logs into the network, the doorman can now also tell them which room group to join and how important their traffic is.

subtitle: Four new RADIUS attributes that let an authentication server hand out VLAN memberships and priority mappings per port.

tldr.problem: Earlier RADIUS guidance (RFC 3580) could assign a VLAN through tunnel attributes, but it did not cover the fuller set of VLAN functions defined by IEEE 802.1Q.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4675 adds attributes 56 to 59: Egress-VLANID, Ingress-Filters, Egress-VLAN-Name and User-Priority-Table, usable in RADIUS or Diameter.
tldr.outcome: A switch can be told which VLANs a port may send on, tagged or untagged, whether to filter ingress, and how to re-map frame priority.

today: RFC 4675 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC has obsoleted or updated it. It builds on RFC 3580 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: Why More VLAN Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 4675 describes Virtual LAN (VLAN) and re-prioritization attributes for provisioning access to IEEE 802 local area networks with RADIUS or Diameter. RFC 3580 already supports VLAN assignment through the tunnel attributes of RFC 2868, but not the fuller VLAN functionality of IEEE 802.1Q.

The new attributes are analogous to the management variables of IEEE 802.1Q and the MIB objects of RFC 4363. They also support a wider range of IEEE 802.1X configurations.
sections.eli5: The old way could only say which one room you belong to. The new attributes let the doorman describe a whole set of rooms and rules.

sections.title: Per-Port, Per-User Scope
sections.content:
The attributes apply to a single NAS port, more precisely an IEEE 802.1Q bridge port, because the IEEE specifications do not recognize finer management than per port. The attributes are applied per user, with one user expected per port. On media such as IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs a "virtual port", usually scoped by station MAC address, may stand in for the physical port.

A NAS that receives an Access-Accept with one of these attributes it cannot apply MUST act as though it had received an Access-Reject. For a CoA-Request (RFC 3576), the NAS replies with a CoA-NAK, and an Error-Cause attribute of "Unsupported Attribute" (401) is recommended. Authorization changes are atomic, so the existing configuration stays unchanged.
sections.eli5: The rules are for one door at a time. If the doorman gives an instruction the door cannot follow, the door stays shut rather than guessing.

sections.title: VLAN Membership Attributes
sections.content:
Egress-VLANID (type 56, length 6) names one VLAN allowed for egress on the port. Its four-octet value has a Tag Indication octet (0x31 tagged, 0x32 untagged), a 12-bit Pad that MUST be zero, and a 12-bit VLANID. Multiple instances may appear, each adding a VLAN to the allowed egress list. Unlike the RFC 3580 tunnel attributes, it sets only egress, not the ingress VLAN for untagged packets (the PVID). To configure an untagged VLAN for both ingress and egress, the tunnel attributes MUST be used.

Ingress-Filters (type 57, length 6) maps to the Ingress Filter variable of IEEE 802.1Q. Value 1 is Enabled and 2 is Disabled. When Enabled, the VLANs allowed to ingress a port must match those allowed to egress it. Only one may be sent per packet.

Egress-VLAN-Name (type 58, length at least 4) works like Egress-VLANID but identifies the VLAN by name. It has a Tag Indication octet (0x31 or 0x32, the ASCII characters '1' and '2') followed by a string. UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED for the name, and a robust implementation SHOULD accept undistinguished octets. When used with the RFC 3580 tunnel attributes, the allowed list is the concatenation of this attribute and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID (81).
sections.eli5: Egress-VLANID is a hall pass listing a room number and whether you wear a name tag there. Egress-VLAN-Name is the same pass, but written with the room's name. Ingress-Filters is a switch that decides if you may only enter rooms you may also leave.

sections.title: Re-mapping Priority
sections.content:
User-Priority-Table (type 59, length 10) carries the IEEE 802.1D regeneration table for a port. IEEE 802 defines eight user priorities, and the table has 8 octets, each an integer from 0 to 7. The first octet gives the regenerated priority for incoming priority 0, the second for incoming priority 1, and so on. The default incoming priority is 0.

This lets a bridge remap incoming priorities, honor them, or override them by forcing all to one chosen priority. A single instance may appear in an Access-Accept or CoA-Request, and it should only be sent to a RADIUS client that supports IEEE 802.1D.
sections.eli5: Imagine mail with a number 0 to 7 for how urgent it is. This attribute is a little chart that says, for each urgency number on arrival, what number to stamp on it instead.

sections.title: Which Packets Carry Them, and Diameter
sections.content:
Egress-VLANID and Egress-VLAN-Name may appear zero or more times in Access-Request, Access-Accept, CoA-Request and Accounting-Request. Ingress-Filters may appear zero or one time in those same packets. User-Priority-Table may appear zero or one time, only in Access-Accept and CoA-Request. None of them may appear in Access-Reject or Access-Challenge.

In Diameter the attributes are AVPs from the RADIUS compatibility code space 1-255, so no new Diameter codes are allocated. Their value types are OctetString (Egress-VLANID and User-Priority-Table), Enumerated (Ingress-Filters) and UTF8String (Egress-VLAN-Name). Gateways between Diameter and RADIUS copy them as is, apart from headers, alignment and padding.

IANA allocated the four attribute numbers 56 to 59 in the existing RADIUS namespace and created no new registries.
sections.eli5: Each note may only be put in certain kinds of envelopes. The same notes also work in the other mail system, Diameter, without changing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The attributes ride inside existing RADIUS packets, protected as described in RFC 3579 and RFC 3576, or in Diameter as specified in RFC 3588. Those protections target spoofing and modification in transit. They do not stop an authorized server or proxy from inserting attributes with malicious intent.

VLAN attributes from such a server or proxy may enable access to unauthorized VLANs. The NAS can limit this with authorization checks, for example accepting only certain VLANIDs from a given server or proxy. A compromised server could also change the user priority table, degrading quality of service by lowering priorities, or causing denial of service by raising priority at many ports and oversubscribing the switch or links.
sections.eli5: The lock on the mailbox keeps strangers out, but not a dishonest doorman. So the building should double-check which rooms any doorman is allowed to hand out.
